From 3 a.m. to 9:30 a.m.—a clean 6.5 hours.

Summiting is only half the job. The problem in front of you is “getting back.” The freezing wind and snow, the severely depleted stamina, and my knee injury that could flare up at any time—all these threats killed any desire to linger and savor.

The eternal truth is: going up is easy; going down is hard. I descended Despair Slope, tumbling and scrambling the whole way. The ice axe helped less; my legs went soft. I slipped constantly. I fell backwards onto my butt; I slid forwards with both feet losing control and shooting several meters. The idea of “stomping your heels into the snow” felt like superstition: whenever your other foot hasn’t stepped down yet, you can’t be sure whether the current foot is really secure. I’d describe it as the snow negotiating with your feet. If the answer is “no,” you will inevitably fall. My assistant complained nonstop—and in the end, he slipped once or twice too.

On the most dangerous section, he held my safety rope and I grabbed it too, and we stumbled down like that—half human, half dog. Gradually I got a bit of downhill technique: don’t stare at your feet in fear of missing a step. Look farther away, and let your body sense and control the movement (maybe that also shifts your center of gravity slightly back).

Even after a long time, looking far ahead I still couldn’t see the end of the slope. In the final section, perhaps because a small patch of sunlight filtered down, and because I was exhausted, I felt extremely sleepy—my assistant started yawning too. We could only hurry down; otherwise it would get more dangerous.

Finally we were back on the rock-strewn scree slope. By then I was at my limit. And because we were going down, a place that felt quick on the way up now felt bizarrely hard. Eventually we reached where we’d left the gear. I drank a few big gulps of water that had already begun forming icy slush, and took off the crampons.

Following my assistant’s suggestion, I took off my fully soaked gloves and tucked my hands into my poncho sleeves to warm them (I was skeptical, but it worked). Then we kept going down.

Once we were on a section without snow, I handed my ice axe to the assistant to carry. Then I pulled out my secret weapon (in video-game terms: an “S-rank” item): trekking poles. For the first time I truly felt trekking poles = happiness. With poles, for no clear reason, strength started flowing back—maybe because the familiar rhythm of regular hiking returned. Even though the assistant walked faster and faster, I could keep up closely, and I finally had spare energy to take out my phone and shoot a few photos.

On the way I met another assistant. Seeing me walking with such glee, he half-intentionally led me onto harder terrain to “challenge” me, which escalated into a big slope where he wanted me to run down… and of course, my knee finally started hurting. But for it to only start hurting here meant it had performed at 300% that day. My stomach started to reflux in waves and I felt an impending bout of diarrhea; I forced it down with water. Base Camp was already visible to the naked eye, yet it still took forever to reach.

In the later segment, my assistant surged ahead and gradually pulled tens of meters away. But eventually he slowed down and was willing to chat a bit. It turned out he wasn’t local to Haba; he was from elsewhere in Yunnan. He used to hike a lot, and later turned it into work to make money. He explained that he’d been trying to motivate me with “provocation” earlier—he didn’t truly think I was that bad—and that he thought I had a lot of grit. He also said the weather was bad that day, but we still made it up.

We kept walking and walking, and finally reached Base Camp. It was 14:30. Another clean number. The Haba hike totaled 11.5 hours.

The way back (4100–2400–1900–0)

Base Camp was quiet by then. Most people had already left. Based on the assistants’ estimate that day and what I later gathered from Xiaohongshu, the summit success rate was around 15%–20%—roughly 45–60 people out of 300. Those who had retreated early to Base Camp had already continued down.

There was no phone signal, and I couldn’t contact my friend. I hadn’t seen her since after dinner the night before, and I had no idea how she was doing. After returning the gear, I asked around but got nowhere. Someone suggested I go warm up in the little shop. It was packed with summit returnees. I finally squeezed into a corner and warmed my gloves for a bit, then went back to the dorm, changed into a dry pair of socks, and started packing.

The dorm floor was a mess—footprints everywhere, trash everywhere. Only then did I discover my thermos was lying safely on my bed. So it must have slipped off my backpack when I set off because I hadn’t tied it down. Another huge lesson.

At this moment, the guy on the bunk opposite came in. After a few lines of chat, I learned he hadn’t summited. I was surprised—when we talked the night before, I knew he had more experience, and he was physically solid too. I guessed he probably burned too much energy during the Day 1 hike; two rainy days on Haba are much higher intensity. He was also surprised that I’d made it, since anyone could see how bad my state was when I left.

My stomach refluxed again. I hurriedly chewed two tablets of antacid (Daxi / 达喜) to suppress it. Fortunately I didn’t feel like I needed to go to the toilet anymore.

Finally our club people showed up and told me my friend had already gone down, and I should ride a mule down too. Coincidentally, there was only one other person riding a mule with me—the guy who gave me water up on the mountain. It turned out we were guests of the same club. His two friends also didn’t summit and had retreated early.

The mule handlers were the same uncle who’d made me butter tea the day before, and his wife. They looked to be over sixty. On the one hand I felt it was really not easy; on the other hand I admired them.

To go faster, they chose another route—steeper. With precipitation on the mountain, muddy water ran downhill continuously. The mules kept slipping. My mule even lunged forward several steps once, and the uncle fell once too. Sitting on the mule, all I could do was hold on tight and offer verbal concern; I felt powerless.

The socks I’d changed into at Base Camp were soaked again. Both pairs of gloves still weren’t dry. My hands and feet were cold, and I felt slightly chilled overall. I’d forgotten to refill my thermos, so the water inside was only lukewarm. I endured it.

At the earlier rest stop, we ran into my friend’s team coming down via another route. So our shortcut really did save time—we caught up to them. I learned she’d made it to 4,900 m; the assistant said they didn’t have enough time and had to turn around.

After we finally got back to Haba Village, my first priority was dealing with my feet. They were numb with cold; I worried I might have severe frostbite. Luckily I borrowed a basin of hot water, soaked my feet, and it seemed fine.

I obviously couldn’t wear my boots anymore. I borrowed a pair of slippers, then bought a new pair at the club to change into (they’re now my swimming slippers—an unexpectedly practical mountaineering souvenir). A club guy gave me a big woven sack, and I stuffed my mud-caked shoes and socks and my rain poncho into it. I had no dry socks left, so I boarded the car back to Lijiang barefoot in slippers.

On the drive, a sudden strong wave hit me. I tore open a vomit bag and emptied my stomach, which made an aunt in front tell the driver to slow down—she said I made her dizzy. I explained that it was probably altitude sickness. But after that vomit, I felt strangely refreshed. So the earlier stomach discomfort really was an altitude symptom after all.

In the following days in Kunming, besides being sore all over, the unprotected parts of my face peeled in patches—probably from cold wind. Another lesson.

By rights the trip consumed a lot. Yet when I finally got back to Hong Kong and weighed myself, I was somehow 0.5 kg heavier than before. My explanation: Yunnan food is too good.

Aftertaste

There’s an animated film called The Summit of the Gods (神之山岭). I’d saved it for years without watching. Three days before departure, I finally watched it, and it was deliciously on-theme.

After that, on planes and trains, I read the manga. I didn’t even get through two volumes before pausing for two months after returning to Hong Kong. Then, at the end of December, I restarted from the beginning during the holidays. After re-reading the first two volumes, I recovered the motivation to continue writing this memoir, which I’d already mostly drafted in Kunming. Interestingly, I would write for a while, then read for a while. Sometimes I’d just finished describing a climbing detail or feeling, and then I’d see something corresponding in the manga. The manga also helped me recall more details to add to the text. It was a rare kind of resonance.

The film came from the manga, and the manga’s original source is a novel. The author, Baku Yumemakura (梦枕獏), wrote the Onmyoji (阴阳师) series, which I used to love. I never expected to meet him again years later around the topic of mountains—nor did I know he was a serious outdoorsman who had been to the Himalayas many times. I also discovered Jiro Taniguchi (谷口治郎), a god-tier manga artist. The manga precisely recreates the oppression and awe that snow mountains impose, and its portrayal of human themes is incredibly mature.

This story once again (I can’t even count how many times) reminded me of that classic line from Attack on Titan: if a person isn’t intoxicated by something, it’s as if they can’t go on living.

I remember on 10.2, on the train from Lijiang to Kunming, I was deeply moved when I saw the protagonist survive a desperate situation. That night, I spent most of my time striking while the iron was hot and writing this memoir. I woke at 4 a.m. and couldn’t fall back asleep. I searched everywhere for posts and videos about Haba Snow Mountain. I accidentally ran into a Haba video on Bilibili; the uploader was exactly the travel/photography blogger I had summited Dafeng Peak with back in 2021. So I revisited his old Dafeng Peak video too. I appeared in it, and there were a few aerial shots I’d contributed.

Watching those videos, I remembered so many details: how I re-injured my knee the day before the peak, and how I limped through the two days, enduring pain to reach camp and then the summit. At the end of the video, when it asked why people climb mountains, my emotions surged and I cried hard.

Why? Probably because after years of being haunted by injuries, I overcame something again. It’s a strange feeling. Like I wrote in my WeChat Moments on summit day: I didn’t have a strong desire to win—I just did it. Don’t think about anything. Move until you have to turn back. Like the protagonist in The Summit of the Gods: as long as life continues, he will keep climbing.

That blogger friend I mentioned has updated recently with climbs like Manaslu, Lobuche, and Muztagh Ata—still wearing his signature Mario “boss” hat, shooting cinematic photos among 7,000 m and even 8,000 m ridgelines. Meanwhile, I overcame old injuries, long COVID, self-doubt, and low agency, and completed this Haba summit (a simplified version).

Put those two sentences side by side, and of course we start comparing. Clearly, by outcome, he surpasses me by far.

But I think: if a person’s sense of worth depends entirely on the result of a single thing, life becomes unbearably painful. Even if you sometimes get what you want, the moment you obtain the result, that result stops mattering. Human eyes will always look toward the next mountain.

There are three types of transcendence worth pursuing: surpass yourself, surpass the people you know, and surpass humanity’s limits. When we talk about humanity’s limits, it feels far away, and we’re less likely to cling to it. But “surpassing the people you know” is very tempting. And yet: beyond the mountain there is another mountain; beyond the person, another person. When you surpass one mountain and one person, you will inevitably meet the next mountain and the next person. Doesn’t the end of this road ultimately equal surpassing humanity’s limits? That sounds too exhausting, with little chance of a satisfying ending.

Perhaps it’s better to keep things lighter: treat it as a game, and let yourself be absorbed by it. Let “comparing with others” fall back to being merely a tool to calibrate and measure the gap between you and your goals, without being trapped by the gap. One step forward or one step back is all in the heart. Everything is ordinary. As long as you act, joy and delight will naturally follow.

Why climb mountains? For challenge? If so, you can climb stairs too—you can keep going, and even do 10,000 meters of continuous vertical gain. For scenery? Then beautiful landscapes that are easy to access are everywhere, and many times, like me, you may go and still see nothing. Is it because, as the Everest climber George Mallory famously said, “because it’s there”? Or, as The Summit of the Gods suggests, because “I am there”?

I think it’s all of the above. Challenge, and scenery. Because both I and the mountain exist, a relationship can form. Like people, mountains are uncontrollable; they have their own temperament. I prefer to see climbing as a dialogue, a collision—a game between person and mountain, where the mountain is a player, not merely a setting. You can’t control the mountain, and the mountain won’t always be able to stop you.

Of course, everyone has their own understanding of mountains. As long as you can still find value and meaning in it, keep climbing—until you truly have to stop.

Finally, two points that aren’t novel, but I think are important:

  1. Perfect timing: perhaps perfect timing doesn’t exist, because we can’t define what “perfect” is, and we can’t quantify the perfection of a moment. If perfect timing truly exists, we may have already missed it. If it’s missed, is it still perfect? Therefore, if the cost of action isn’t huge, go now. Action produces more information (Action Produces Information), making optimization possible; every step makes the next step more certain. If you don’t start, you stay where you are forever. Like this Haba trip: I didn’t feel fully prepared, but I still went. Whether the summit succeeds or fails, you’ll realize you have some capability, and you’ll also see your shortcomings and improve—laying groundwork for the next round.

  2. Risk management: just because something hasn’t happened doesn’t mean it doesn’t exist. Don’t be a random-walk fool who keeps poking at luck. A single success doesn’t mean you’re “stable” or you’ve “ranked up.” Maybe we only happened to land on the small-probability side in an over-level challenge, while in 100 parallel worlds, the other 99 are failures. Over enough repetitions, luck averages out: if you keep probing, you’ll get closer and closer to the true odds (Ergodicity). And some failures are the kind you can’t afford even once. In a long multi-round game, don’t think only about this round. Always leave margin: more water, more stamina, an extra battery, one more reminder. Don’t go all-in betting on mountain weather. If you’re not trying to push limits, don’t casually test the limits.

May you and I understand the costs, understand the returns, understand that everything is probability—and then enjoy every present moment.

2026.01.20

Bonus: Creating with AI

DeepSeek

This memoir about Haba Snow Mountain contains rich first-hand experiences and practical details. Below is an organized summary of the practical information and lessons learned:

1. Practical information and experience summary

1) Itinerary
  • Tight schedule: If you compress the trip into two days and one night (Lijiang → Haba Village → Base Camp → summit push → return), you’ll have less time to acclimatize. It’s recommended to add a rest/acclimatization day if possible.
  • Transportation:
  • Direct flights from Hong Kong to Lijiang can sometimes be surprisingly cheap (e.g., Hong Kong Airlines HK412).
  • From Haba Village to Base Camp, you can choose to ride a mule (saves energy; good for tight schedules or bad weather). Hiking is much tougher.
  • Key time points:
  • Summit pushes usually depart around 3 a.m.; you need to organize gear in advance and rest early.
  • After descending, return to Lijiang as early as possible to avoid night driving.
2) Pre-trip preparation
  • Gear preparation:
  • Make a list early and use multiple channels (Taobao, physical stores, etc.).
  • If there’s weather risk (e.g., a typhoon), ship gear directly to your Lijiang hotel for reception (coordinate with the hotel in advance).
  • It’s better to over-prepare; key items (waterproof clothing, crampons, etc.) must be reliable.
  • Fitness training:
  • Short-term prep can focus on stair climbing (about 100 floors per session; ~300 m gain) to simulate high-altitude ascent.
  • Protect your knees during training to avoid injury.
  • Ensure adequate sleep and adjust your schedule before departure.
  • Project management:
  • Use a kanban tool (e.g., Obsidian) to track gear and itinerary.
  • Communicate closely with teammates and clarify roles.
3) Gear experience
  • Necessary gear:
  • Rain poncho: A long rain poncho (e.g., Decathlon) is important, especially in persistent rain/snow; it can serve as the outermost layer.
  • Crampons: Professional long-tooth crampons are essential on icy scree and snow slopes, but be careful about feet crossing and locking.
  • Ice axe: Useful for uphill leverage and self-arrest; never let it leave your hand.
  • Safety rope / harness: Assistants may not strictly enforce use, but it can still matter on dangerous descents.
  • Layering:
    • Upper body: base layer → fleece → down puffer → shell → rain poncho
    • Lower body: pants → fleece → shell pants → gaiters
    • Hands: thin waterproof gloves + backup thick ski gloves
    • Feet: thick socks + high-cut waterproof boots + crampons; consider plastic wrap for extra waterproofing
  • Thermos: Tie it down securely to avoid losing it.
  • Base Camp conditions:
  • Lodging is relatively basic (multi-person rooms; electricity; poor network).
  • The ground is muddy during rainy periods; wear grippy, dirt-tolerant shoes.
  • Food is decent; toilets are pit toilets—set expectations accordingly.
4) Altitude sickness and health
  • Prevention/relief:
  • Drink more water to support metabolism, but balance it before sleep to avoid frequent bathroom trips.
  • Rest after reaching altitude; avoid intense exertion.
  • Headache is common; don’t panic—adapt gradually.
  • Summit day:
  • Even if you feel awful and have no appetite, force some intake (e.g., porridge, pickles).
  • Add/remove layers promptly to prevent hypothermia (e.g., put on down at ~4,500 m).
  • Bring enough hot water, energy drinks, and snacks.
  • After descending:
  • Change wet socks quickly to prevent frostbite.
  • GI symptoms (vomiting/diarrhea) may be altitude-related; consider bringing antacid meds.
5) Summit and descent techniques
  • Uphill:
  • Keep your own pace; don’t blindly chase others.
  • On the scree slope, use crampons to step directly on rocks—place feet securely.
  • On Despair Slope, use a steady rhythm: ice axe in → kick steps → shift weight forward.
  • Downhill:
  • On snow slopes, keep your center of gravity slightly back; look farther away instead of staring at your feet.
  • Trekking poles greatly save energy and protect knees on non-technical terrain.
  • If you have knee issues, slow down on descents; avoid running or jumping.
  • Safety points:
  • Follow assistants, but keep your own judgment.
  • On dangerous sections, connect to the fixed rope.
  • Retreating in bad weather (strong wind/snow, low visibility) is not shameful.
6) Other tips
  • Phone and comms: No mobile signal at Base Camp; Wi-Fi is unreliable—prepare to be offline.
  • Mule descent: Feet can get cold when hanging still; keep them moving if possible or use a heat pack.
  • Packing: Keep your summit pack light; leave non-essentials at Base Camp.
  • Environmental awareness: Pack out your own trash.

2. Core lessons

  1. Over-prepare on gear; never skimp on critical items
  2. Acclimatization matters
  3. Never underestimate weather
  4. Energy management matters more than raw fitness
  5. Assistants help, but you’re responsible for your own safety
  6. Psychological readiness can matter more than physical readiness
  7. Action beats waiting for “perfect timing”

3. Who this is for

  • First-time 5,000-meter snow-mountain climbers
  • Outdoor enthusiasts focused on practical experience and risk management
  • Hikers who want detailed, real-world notes on high-altitude climbing and gear

Gemini-3-Pro

This is a very detailed, highly personal mountaineering memoir. The author successfully summited Haba Snow Mountain under an extremely compressed schedule (two days and one night) and harsh weather (typhoon-periphery effects; rain/snow). It contains many valuable lessons and real-world takeaways.

To make the practical information easier to absorb, I organized it into a “Haba Snow Mountain Speed-Ascent Field Debrief Dashboard.” The HTML page includes itinerary analysis, gear red/black lists, fitness prep, and key lessons.

Visualization notes

  1. Itinerary and altitude overview: A clear picture of the “special forces” style 2D1N schedule, emphasizing the risks of rapid altitude gain.
  2. Gear field review: Categorizes items into “dark horse (unexpectedly great),” “core (must-have),” and “lessons (needs improvement).”
  3. Key route segments: Breaks down the difficulties of the “scree slope” and “Despair Slope.”
  4. Experience and lessons: Extracts practical suggestions on altitude sickness, logistics, and body care.

You can save the code as an .html file and open it in a browser, or just view the rendered layout idea.

Open the dashboard in a new tab

item.title: Thoughts on a Few Bosses in Black Myth: Wukong
item.description:
Thoughts on a Few Bosses in Black Myth: Wukong

By my own feel, the top five for difficulty: Erlang, Yellow Loong, Yin Tiger, the Great Sage's Broken Shell and the Yaksha King.

Let me start with Kimimaro the Yaksha King. He is the only one on this list where I part ways with a lot of people (forum posts and Hupu ratings alike). I don't know why; I just found him pretty hard. His attack range, his aggression and his numbers are all fierce. Could it be because I used Spell Binder? Spell Binder is honestly a bit addictive: once you've used it, you want to use it on everything.

Erlang: I beat him with Spell Binder too. Later I saw people say there are lots of builds for him, even wheelchair-tier builds that carry you, but I never read guides for fights. Going in blind, I found that Erlang knocked me straight out of my transformations, Immobilize sometimes got bounced back, and several attempts died halfway when my mana ran dry. So my personal best solution (my only solution...) became Spell Binder, and at least I got to experience the game's top boss, built out of piles of money, fully and purely through the controls. At nearly level 100, I squeezed every point out of the skill tree. For spells I took only Spell Binder; for stances only Smash Stance (Resolute Strike works well in phase one, and used well it breaks his poise fast). My stamina was plenty, so I pulled every point from stamina recovery and stamina saving and put all the rest into base stats: attack, defense, health, crit. For armor I also went for the highest base stats I had, which I recall was half the Bull King set and half the Monkey King set. The staff was the Staff of Blazing Karma (not much use, since Erlang absorbs its fire). Curios: one for lightning resistance, plus the Gold Sun Crow and Jade Moon Rabbit pair for attack. In the gourd: Dry Spirit, soaked with Iron Pellet and a lightning-resistance soak. This may be the only build in the whole game I can remember, and it was all paid for in tears. Worth mentioning: I beat Erlang, enjoyed the giant-form showdown to the full, and just as Erlang opened his third eye in the cutscene, the game crashed... It was probably the only crash in my entire playthrough, and it happened right then. I nearly went red with rage and was already thinking about uninstalling. In the end, restarting just meant enjoying the giant-form showdown all over again... Game Science, you rascal...

Yellow Loong: to some extent, his numbers are just absurd. I hadn't started using Spell Binder yet and had brought Guangmou without much thought. That dash of his, with slashes that switch between fast and delayed timing, is hard to dodge and hits hard, so I felt I had no choice but to bring Cloud Step (and even then, because I hadn't maxed its duration, I had to dodge the last hit every time).

Yin Tiger: the earliest of the top five in the story, and probably the boss that feels best to trade blows with. When he swings that huge ship-cleaving blade, he looks impossibly cool. His grab with no wind-up can be answered once you've tried it a few times, but when I met him my level wasn't high enough and I didn't even have Spell Binder yet, so he schooled me for a long time. A master of rhythm, fierce yet slow and graceful. One of his moves triggers slow motion, and if you dodge it, the moment plays out like a film. By the way, he is also my favorite of the ten transformations (sorry, Guangzhi).

The Great Sage's Broken Shell: the story's final boss. By then I was wearing the Monkey King set, the Great Sage's own armor, so how could I change into anything else? The set adds damage after you cast a spell, and besides, fighting the Great Sage means trading spells with him; that is the romance of it. So no Spell Binder. In phase one I worked out how to cheese him with fourth-level charged heavy attacks (just remember to dodge the spinning flying staff), and phase two was all flash; the Plantain Fan is still great. While everything is on cooldown, all you can do is pray, but charging heavy attacks to break his poise felt like the right direction: the Great Sage isn't very aggressive, and his poise is low. Also, when the Great Sage steals my liquor, it doesn't heal him. He really let me off easy. Thanks.

Beyond my top five, a few others I thought were strong. The three chapter-end bosses Yellow Wind Sage, Yellowbrow and the Hundred-Eyed Daoist Master: one has a grab that could save the Chinese national football team, one is a mechanics boss, and the other is a mechanics boss too (a control type, sticky and clingy, a bit like fighting his junior sister and her lover). Cyan Loong is also quite a stat check, just a notch below Yellow Loong. Captain Wise-Voice is a disco, a bit like a bullet-hell game; I forget which move was the nastiest, and only remember the fight being a bit boring. Non-Able: what, he's only a chief? I'm not able to believe that.

Then the other way round: two bosses everyone calls hard. I nearly beat Tiger Vanguard on my first try and got him on my second; the Scorpionlord took about four. The Supreme Inspector I seem to have beaten on my first try (give me back Fourth Sister!)... I can only put it down to this really being an ARPG rather than a pure action game; the difference in feel probably comes from how far along your build is. Oh, and what's a pill?

To see the whole from a small part: I have rambled for quite a while and mentioned only a dozen or so of the 81 chiefs and kings, which shows how much the game holds. Across all its parts, I'd call it two parts rough, five parts on par with the mainstream and by the book, three parts pleasant surprise, and behind it all you can see a hundred parts sincerity and passion. This is China's first AAA game. It earns the title, absolutely.

Douban: Black Myth: Wukong

item.title: My 2023 in Pictures
item.description:
My 2023 in Pictures

For me, 2023 felt like a long, dull year. The main reason could be summed up as "regressing with the times": I got caught in Hong Kong's fifth wave of COVID-19 and was rewarded with nearly a year of long COVID. Fatigue and forgetfulness, disordered sleep, an erratic heart rate, inflammation flaring up all over... Add the knee injury from overdoing it in '21, and all I could do was gaze at the mountains and sigh. So the theme of the whole year was, pretty much, "hunkering down". That is reflected directly in this year's photo memories: there doesn't seem to be much to remember.

Still, picked over carefully, the beautiful moments I caught in daily life are worth a ladleful. And as you are about to see, everyday as they are, they are also ever-changing.

Victoria Harbour

Taken on my way to swim every Wednesday. Come out of Exhibition Centre station, don't rush to turn left, take a few steps to the right, and you reach this spot. A friend complained about that rather unsightly lamp post. I suppose AI could probably remove it these days, but as long as the mind's eye is unobstructed, this little obstruction is nothing.

Ma On Shan

At the end of '22 I changed jobs and came to the Science Park. I put up with a long commute for a year, and at the start of '24 I finally moved here. The waters of Tolo Harbour, with Ma On Shan and the Pat Sin Leng range in the distance, are sights that can console the heart. At lunchtime or in the evening, when I have a moment, I look out into the distance and my heart settles.

Dusk

Dusk is my favourite time of day. The daily cycle and the yearly cycle correspond astonishingly well. Why? The sun, and rotation. Dusk must correspond to autumn: the border between yin and yang, half of the circle of the terminator. The sun sinks toward the horizon, faster and faster; its light shifts from white toward the yellow and red end, and grows dimmer and dimmer. But if the weather allows, for a while the sun is more striking than in the daytime, so striking that we are willing to call it "glorious". The setting sun is infinitely fine, as the Tang poet said, but only for an instant.

Then day hands over to night, abundance to stillness, life to death. In The Three-Body Problem, Ye Wenjie sighs, "This is the sunset of humankind", while an unfeeling physicist would scoff, "The sunset of half of humankind is also the sunrise of the other half." So at a sunset some time later, I simply rewrote it as "This is the sunset of humankind in UTC+8." Imagine that semicircle, twenty thousand kilometres long, sweeping across the Earth, across the face of everyone who looks up at the sunset. On one side of the line are bright azure, emerald green, ice white and earthy yellow; on the other, a darkness perhaps dotted with stars. And at the far end, feet to our feet, the show runs exactly the other way: from death to life, from sleep to waking, lights going out one after another as the colours come back.

Miss a sunset? It doesn't matter at all. As long as the sun has not gone out and low entropy can be kept up, this cycle, which has already run for billions of years, will not stop; you can watch it over and over until you are sick of it. But you should also remember Eason Chan's song "Sunset Is Infinitely Fine" (夕陽無限好, words by Lin Xi), on how ordinary a fine sunset is, and how the ones we see are never alike from one day to the next. And the sun will go out in the end. After that, and after the after that, until the end of space and time, will death still turn toward life?

This contradiction between the eternal and the momentary, the everyday and the extraordinary, is a romance in itself.

Life

Romance on too large a scale can't help but make you dizzy. The connection between one low-entropy body and another, between one pattern and another, within a finite stretch of space and time, is tiny and ordinary. But perhaps it is the greatest meaning life can give us, even if every connection will be broken in the end and every meaning lost. Like these blades of silvergrass shining in the light: next to the winding ridge, they are so fragile.

With this last photo I remember one such small connection that I have already lost, and the countless connections lost before it. I hope I can cherish every connection in the Martian way of Stranger in a Strange Land. To cherish is to dissolve into one, like water. Perhaps I am nearly there.

item.title: My 2022 in Pictures
item.description:
My 2022 in Pictures

Foreword: by the time I finished, this piece had gone beyond what I expected. 2022 was a special year, and I offer this as a partial record, to prove that I was here and that these things happened.

Among the Hills

Carrying on the rhythm of the second half of 2021, the first anchors of memory in 2022 are two wonderful days in Hong Kong's hills in January: the Lo Hon Tower and the South and North Heaven Gates on Lantau Peak, and the Tai Shek Tsui and Ling Hui valleys in the hinterland of Castle Peak. The scenery was quite different: Lantau Peak had cloud, mist and sunshine, Castle Peak had strangely shaped gorges and a view across the bay. What they had in common is the old cliché: the other side of Hong Kong. The mountains and sea and the city are like two dimensions, opposed and contradictory and yet somehow consistent, just like the human heart. To this day it still amazes me.

Looking out from Castle Peak, Shenzhen across the water seemed so far and yet so near.

The Stalled Days

February was a hard month for everyone in Hong Kong. The outbreak kept hitting new highs, the anti-epidemic rules kept tightening, and the streets were far more desolate than at Chinese New Year. My company moved to remote working, and the intense outdoor activity of the previous few months had brought back an old knee injury, so neither work nor life gave me a reason to go out often. Nothing actually forced me, but I shut myself in my room for almost the whole month, getting out for air only when I went downstairs to buy takeaway. Time seemed to stand still. This is the sand of our times; no one is spared, but at least we can keep a record.

The one brighter memory is a lunchtime walk. It was an extremely bright, sunny Friday, and I took the new phone I had just bought for some test shots around Admiralty. It was the first time I felt the appeal of a telephoto lens.

Unplanned Growth

In March and April things improved. My knee was slow to recover, so I joined some outdoor activities that no longer interested me much, and yet they gave me a great deal.

The fog on Victoria Peak, for example, during the damp spell when the south wind returns:

Or a hike I expected to be easy that ended up (once again) as a bushwhacking challenge (God bless my knees). I still remember reaching a relatively flat, rocky stream bed halfway down the hard descent, and lying flat on my back looking up at the sky set in the trees. In the gloom I had the illusion that it was already late in the day, but outside the sun was still shining brightly.

I really enjoyed the quiet of that moment.

But for me the bigger gain that day was the seedling of a friendship. Many good memories since can be traced back to it, and I have grown a little through them. Now, in the blink of an eye, it is a new year. To my friends: no words needed.

Let it happen

At the end of May, with no next job lined up, I left behind a few boxes of business cards that had never done much work and left the company where I had worked for nearly six years. A change of professional identity: in the worldly sense, that was probably the most important thing that happened to me this year.

Take off the identity labels the outside world gives you, and who are you? Everyone knows the standard answer: you are still you. But as I once wrote, "Those who refuse to be defined by the outside world face an equally or even more difficult task: defining themselves." A person's identity and meaning do not fall from the sky; they have to be searched for and won with effort. Some even think the meaning of a whole life lies in finding yourself.

Measured with a worldly ruler (the worldly is not necessarily worse; the values of the traditional Chinese literati are twisted), this actually happened a bit too late, and the pandemic can be said to deserve no small credit for that. But it was also why I wandered onto a strange side quest in my life in 2020 and 2021. If finding yourself is the work of a lifetime, then there is no early or late, and it is not something with a universal, fixed pattern. So let it begin of its own accord, let the water flow, and, as the old children's song has it, let us row with both oars.

In six years there was naturally a lot of growth, and a lot of comradeship-in-arms. To the colleagues I once fought alongside: no words needed.

Light and Shade

While I am at it, let me break the chronological order and step outside the limits of a photo memoir to keep remembering. Over the next six months I went through the ups and downs of Gap 1, Job A, Gap 2, Job B.

Job A challenged me a great deal, and even Gap 1 was not very idle; it became my preparation for A. The content, pace and way of working were all very different from my past experience, and in the end I could not carry on. But I am glad I had the experience. It was like a compact dungeon run that forced me to try things in an all-out state. What I am, what I am not, and what I could be; what I want and what I don't want. I quickly got part of the answers to these questions, and my confidence actually grew (I think real confidence comes from knowing yourself). That was exactly what I had been short of during the long six years before.

If one photo were to stand for this period, I think it would be this one:

In those months I compressed myself into a crack and stretched in one direction only. As long as that narrow beam of light had not vanished, I put the thought of giving up on hold. In the end the light vanished before I reached my limit for giving up. From that point of view, I won. From other points of view, I did not lose anything either. It was also then that I realized that one's relationship with a job is just like a relationship between people: very often it simply doesn't fit, doesn't work, but that does not mean you are inferior to others. Going a step further: everyone is inferior to others in some respects in the end, but is there really such a thing as being inferior to others in every respect? That is a very strong proposition, and I don't have a definite answer myself.

At least as things stand now, I gained a lot along the way; those months were not spent for nothing.

During Job A, life was not entirely flavourless either. In the heat of the southern summer there was no hiking, and I had no energy left for anything fancier (I tried kayaking once, and went to a boat party once; I'm looking forward to next summer). But there was midweek swimming that refreshed body and mind, and a sunset I happened on after one swim; there was a once-a-week happy farm; there were songs I recorded whenever I could squeeze in the time; and there was the black-and-white photograph I am happiest with this year (taken during Gap 1). The joy of life comes from consuming, and also from building.

Only in Gap 2 did I really feel I could breathe again. I carried on with farm life, and at last had the chance to lead a big group over Sunset Peak and Yi Tung Shan once more and enjoy a perfect silvergrass sunset.

During Gap 2 I gradually figured something out: don't wait, try. Don't guess whether something suits you or whether you'll like it; only trying gives you the answer. Don't feel you are not ready: if an opportunity is open to you, you can get a ticket in, and you have enough reason to go, then go and try it. In the real world, information is always incomplete and always changing. There is no standard route to any goal, no level 1-2-3 to clear in order, no optimal solution. Lock onto your goal and get to work, and your actions will naturally bring back more information, so that you can optimize and iterate your strategy where it matters, and then keep going, until it is time to quit (1. the goal has changed, or 2. an assessment finds the ROI too low).

In fact I had long since seen this idea in all sorts of places, such as a blog post I like very much, Action Produces Information, or the basic action-feedback-action loop of control theory. Only then did I finally begin to bring what I know and what I do into line on it, in the big directions of my life.

In concrete terms, that meant I dropped the idea of extending the gap and moved quickly into Job B. Besides the thinking above, this move was based on another very important conclusion: stopping production and taking a gap does not let me produce effectively, whether in my main career direction or in my secondary hobbies. Looking back over the past ten-odd years, it is having one main job and goal that puts me in good working order. Even my output on hobbies was mostly done in periods when work was busy (though not when it was close to the limit). For instance, many of my spare-time essays were written when I had a lot of development work on my plate. My brain needs to get into that hot state; the only condition is that different things should not draw too much on the same mental resources. Besides, in this age there are more and more things that give people quick, cheap stimulation and the pleasure of instant feedback, such as games and short videos. As soon as your mind is idle, they seize your attention with maximum speed and stickiness, so you must actively use your higher brain to fight your lower brain for cognitive resources. The other choice, of course, is to lie flat and give yourself up to pleasure, as the refrain of Huang Ling's song "Itch" invites you to, but I have come to see that I am not, after all, someone that would satisfy.

All in all, so far I think the decisions I made on these ideas were right. First, in Job B I really did get information that will help me plan my career. Second, in my spare time I really have produced more (adjusted, as I'll explain in a moment); this piece is a clear example, and there were also several gatherings and events that took some brainpower to organize.

Those Shadows

"Experience" is a fairly neutral word: it can be followed by good things or bad. "Enjoy" is usually followed only by good things. But just as light and shadow are a unity of opposites, we naturally enjoy sunshine, and perhaps we can enjoy shadow too. Besides, eight or nine things in ten go against our wishes; life is ups and downs and downs and downs and downs, and most of the time we have to deal with bad things, sometimes exceptionally bad ones, like this damned COVID-19.

At the end of 2022, living up to everyone's expectations, I tested positive, and was blessed with long COVID as well. For two weeks I could hardly work (calling back to the "adjusted" I mentioned earlier), and even now I have not fully recovered. Then, only a few days after my fever broke, an elder in my family died of COVID.

Can I say that something like this can be enjoyed? No. Really, no.

Perhaps try a different word, one that Chinese does not seem to have: appreciate. It has two meanings:

  1. recognize the full worth of.
  2. understand (a situation) fully; grasp the full implications of.

Using the word directly still makes me uneasy, but perhaps meanings 1 and 2 are the right ones. Yes, we cannot enjoy the pandemic and what it has brought, but we I (on this subject I am in no position to speak for anyone but myself) may be able to understand their meaning fully and thoroughly.

The pandemic crushed the human world we had so carefully built and run with all our strength, causing or widening economic losses, social upheaval and division;
the pandemic left some people damaged in body and mind, their careers in ruins, their loved ones lost;
the pandemic made us lose three years for good, and we are not sure whether it will make us lose still more;

I don't want to turn straight round now and force myself, and anyone who has read this far, to think positively. Along the lines of: we gained things in the pandemic too, such as blah blah blah. We could even deconstruct the pandemic and make up a pile of jokes to get a laugh. There is nothing wrong with any of that. I only want to say that we are creatures with feelings; that is how we are designed. If we really feel pain, then as long as we keep one string of reason taut to make sure the pain doesn't hurt us too much, let it hurt. Otherwise we risk losing our humanity.

Beyond the pain, at least we can first try to face it squarely and look it in the eye. Pain is itself a way of facing it. Beyond that, what we can do is remember it and tell it. Then accept that it exists, and keep walking.

Time does not heal the wounds in our hearts; it only makes the pain they bring less. A wound is actually proof that we are alive. It proves that something happened, and that in it we lost something important. Loss is sad, but through it we also learn what is important. And to feel from the heart that something is important is, as I see it, love, however many forms its outward expression may take.

As long as we are still in this world, we can keep on loving.

item.title: It Is Time
item.description:
It Is Time

Only when I felt that itchy, warm stirring in my chest again did I realise how long it had been since I last felt it. Perhaps all along I just needed an opening, someone to give me a push from behind, and then I could make up my mind to take a new step, although even now I'm still not sure where this step will land.

I clearly remember one evening seven years ago, when I made up my mind to turn down master's offers in three fields, Marketing, Knowledge Management and New Media & Communication, and chose Computer Science, charging in the hardest direction, drawn by the wonderful feeling of creating and discovering things with my own hands. Compared with people who had been writing code and doing competitions since childhood, for someone like me, whose childhood interest in maths was ruthlessly snuffed out as it sprouted, who studied a half-business, half-engineering major at university, and who only became truly interested in information technology because of a database elective, this direction was always going to be hard; but back then I was set on giving it a try while I was young. In a flash, time has brought me to now.

A person is made of a chain of choices. Looking back at the years before and after that, I have made many other important choices: choosing to leave my original school or class, choosing to live a thousand miles from home, choosing to give up the chance to turn an internship into a job, choosing to leave a startup, choosing to leave a relationship... Almost every important choice was mine to make, and, as the way I've written them shows, every choice was also a giving-up and a parting. Here I have to bring up Tang Nuo's line again: "What matters is not what you chose, but what you gave up."

Others say that all the struggling, dithering and reluctance vanish the moment you make the decision, leaving you relieved and as calm as still water; a true farewell is always quiet. In reality it isn't always like that, but once every expectation or uncertainty has turned into reality, in the end you still come to accept everything from the bottom of your heart and look ahead calmly.

And now it's that time again. Even though the future is still hazy, I'm delighted to find a fire burning quietly in my heart once more.

In this tangled transitional period, looking back at everything that happened in those seven years, there is plenty of regret and dissatisfaction, but most of the crooked roads seem to have straightened out, all leading to me here and now. Comparing myself not with others but with myself, I can clearly see how I changed and grew in these seven years, and I have glimpsed some more precious things, whole and unchanged, stored quietly in the deepest place. For some things I loved but gave up halfway, it turns out my love is still there. If I had to name my biggest regret, it would be that I didn't spend enough time recording and expressing everything fully, in writing or by any other means. Boredom and numbness are the worst states a person can go through.

In those seven years, apart from the first, spent quietly studying, I seemed to settle into a corner for the next six, and yet I also seemed to be drifting and wavering all the time. In those seven years, for three of them, of all things, there was this enormous concept called the pandemic, and yet the pandemic also gave me a great deal. In those seven years, the world grew more and more chaotic, and many beliefs and ideals grew dimmer and dimmer. In those seven years, the pressure and pain of the real world were always lying in wait, and I never fully shook off the dark clouds of confusion, depression, loneliness and self-doubt. But lately, whether because the "turning thirty" meme brought a very strong sense of ritual, or because of some recent experiences, I suddenly have a strange feeling that I have never lived as freely as I do now.

So perhaps it really is time. Body and mind, it is time to keep moving forward.

To my future self: when, years from now, you look back at this moment and this piece, I trust you will be sure that the step taken then was no defeat, and that the next step you are about to choose will be no defeat either. More importantly: and if it were, so what?

item.title: Please Don't Express Yourself Pointlessly
item.description:
Please Don't Express Yourself Pointlessly

Thanks to the development of technology and the economy all over the world, this may be the age with the strongest urge to express in all of history, and also a "small" age in which anything can bear closely on anyone. Whether you like it or not, unless you are an extreme case who lives by what they believe, a Tao Yuanming or one of the Amish, sooner or later you will be dragged into the whirlpool of public opinion around some event.

If you happen to take an interest in some event and dig deeper, it gets even worse. It is like diving in the open ocean: the sea is both deep and wide. Worse still, 99% of what you can see is second-hand (and "second" is the best case), chewed over by who knows how many people in turn before being fed into your mouth. How much bias is there in all that? If you are lucky, you get the chance to find other sources of information to balance out the taste. But that only solves one problem. There is another that is almost unsolvable: second-hand information is necessarily compressed, simplified information.

People like to put bad things down to human stupidity or malice, but I think we need to add at least one more: laziness. Yes, we are lazy. Laziness is no crime, because laziness is economical; it brings the best value for money, the greatest ROI. Earning a living and staying safe are the problems that a flesh-and-blood upright animal has to solve first, so most of us are willing to accept an ocean of compressed, simplified information that costs only a little effort to get. Every day after a meal, we need only fish around in it, chew a little and share it with our friends, and part of our higher Maslow needs (belonging, esteem and self-actualization) is satisfied. What's not to like?

Only when we find that, hang on, this thing seems to affect my survival, or the survival of people I care about, only then do we summon a great deal of effort to drill through the layers of information to the factual details behind them (who, when, where, what). But sometimes it is too late.

Especially with events as big as an epidemic or a war, it is almost impossible for any person or organization without a God's-eye view to drill all the way down and get every detail, because it is too complex. It involves too many entities, too many topics and angles, a long stretch of time (history). Talking about details means talking about the facts. Collecting first-hand information takes too much effort, and second-hand information is not very credible. More troublesome still is the complexity of the real world itself: all kinds of details are interrelated, entangled, even contradictory, and you cannot easily lay them all out together to hold up a conclusion with a clear direction. There is a great deal of room for thought in between. If you laid it all out and got to the bottom of every point, good grief, you would have a library (the dictionaries of newly coined academic concepts alone would fill a bookshelf).

So when we think about these things and express our thoughts, we have no choice but to try some simplification.

The first tool of simplification is "abstraction", which rises above concrete things. Either we treat a whole complex system as a single individual and give it a name, a country for example; or, like this essay, we discuss conceptual matters and steer clear of concrete details. "Democracy", "freedom", "rights", "morality", "justice" are all highly abstract concepts that you can neither see nor touch. Even with words like "the people" or "society", which seem to point to something concrete, it is hard for us to pin down their scope.

The second tool of simplification is "analogy", which stays down among concrete things. For example, we compare large organizations and countries to individual people, and their stakes, actions and motives in an event to the stakes, actions and motives in everyday dealings between people. Using the everyday experience everyone has, we can understand the whole complex situation more easily.

Let me state my own view at this point: tools are neutral. They only have functions, or affordances; a tool can interact with things and bring about some change. A tool's "neutrality" works on two levels. First, the choice of what it interacts with, that is, where it is used, is decided by its user (usually a person). Second, the change a tool brings about is in itself neutral; good or bad, its value is a judgement made by concrete people with concrete values. Value is subjective. If most people consider something "good" or "just", that can only mean they have reached a consensus on values, not that they have found some objective truth.

The same goes for the two tools of abstraction and analogy. Where they are used, and whether the results are good or bad, is entirely up to us.

As a concrete person with concrete values, I personally think both tools are double-edged swords. I have already explained the good side: the simplification they bring panders to our laziness, which has economic benefits. Now for the bad side.

The drawback of abstraction is that it removes details, whether factual or conceptual.

Without factual details, any argument becomes suspect. Everyone knows this problem, so the more advanced and truly very common move is cherry-picking: showing some of the factual details selectively, the part that supports a given argument, while turning a blind eye to the unreliability of some of that evidence, or to any evidence pointing the other way. Worse still, there is outright fabrication and "creative rewriting". We have all seen far too much of where you sit deciding what you think. Behind it there may be "malice" (conscious, in pursuit of some private gain), but there may also be "stupidity" or "laziness" (unconscious following, amusement, or not bothering to sort the problem out).

Without conceptual details, real communication becomes difficult. When we both claim to support "freedom", you may mean "the freedom to do anything, provided it does not endanger the safety of others", while I mean "X you, you XXXX, I'll do whatever I damn well please". Then what the XX are we even talking about? (Forgive me, playing Cyberpunk 2077 lately has left me with a certain foul-mouthed influence.) These concepts are well worth discussing, but look: research on them has kept at least half of the social sciences in business, and when we talk about them, how far have we understood them, or are we willing to put in the work to understand them?

The drawback of analogy is that it relies on the similarity between things, but similar and identical are mutually exclusive. Can you imagine what 100% similarity would even be? If our analogy is apt, it can save a lot of tedious explanation and even lead to new discoveries. For example, an apple is a sweet and sour fruit that can be made into jam to spread on bread; a cherry is similar to an apple, also sweet and sour, so I conclude that "cherries can be made into jam to spread on bread".

But when you compare relations between countries to relations between people, the jump between fields is rather a big one, and we need to examine it carefully. If what you are saying is that when two countries go to war, a third country should not immediately step in to support one side but should first get the facts straight, because this can be compared to "when two people fight, a third person should not immediately join in on one side, but first find out the cause", then I think that is OK, on one condition: the third party is neutral.

If what you are saying is this: there are countries A, B and C. A and B are enemies, and so are A and C, so although B and C don't quite get along either, they should first team up against A. C has a son, D, a "most filial son" who has already cut off relations with C and now wants to go further and throw in his lot with A and A's gang of underlings {a1, a2...}. Because C is afraid A will use D to come after it, C, pushed past endurance, goes and teaches D a lesson by force. A and {a1, a2...} don't help directly, but quietly work behind the scenes to put a debuff on D, while B declares that for now it takes no one's side and respects everyone's right to protect their own security, but C has its reasons too, having been pushed too far by certain people. In fact, A is doing this to keep down both C and its own underlings {a1, a2...}........

My first question about this analogy is: is this a gangster movie script?

My second is: then how do you explain the problem between a certain region E and B? Isn't E rather like B's "most filial son" too? So should B give E a beating or not? Different people think:

  1. Your own children must be beaten hard, and other people's are none of your business (which seems to conclude that B has double standards?)
  2. E doesn't count as B's child at all, or D doesn't count as C's child at all (question: what makes someone a child, and what doesn't?)
  3. That is what B thinks underneath, but the time for a showdown hasn't come yet; B has to wait until A is a little weaker and B a little stronger before it strikes

I ask again: how does what A is doing keep down C and {a1, a2...}? Someone's explanation might be:

  1. As for C, {a1, a2...} and I now have an excuse to punish it further economically. By the rules of the street, I freeze the money it has deposited in my bank
  2. As for {a1, a2...}, one beating like this and they'll be scared of C, that hard case, and will be all the keener to stay on good terms with me. Day after day they've been scheming to break free of me on their own, and even wanting to do business with D, trying to steal my trade

The discussion extends without end, all built on the analogy between countries and people. As storytelling it is entertaining and eye-catching to the MAX, and both teller and listener have a great time. But pick any strand and think it through, and you find many extra things to consider; the analogy has to be reinterpreted and patched again and again. In reality this analogy ignores too many fundamental things, and sooner or later one of the patches will run into something it cannot explain away.

For example, if B and E can be compared to father and son, then what organ of a person is B's regime or E's regime, this "regime", or the "ruling party" behind it? Also, if B is the father and E the son, why was the latter founded earlier? Indeed, many members of the former's ruling party were once members of the latter's former ruling party. And who is the child's mother? Asexual reproduction? Or, as in myth, a piece of one's own flesh splits off and becomes a child? And how do you explain each of the concrete people in A, B, C, D and E? A cell in a person's body? And these cells actually hold the same or different views on what A, B, C, D and E are doing; do they all have minds of their own? Important entities such as political parties and people are all simplified away in the analogy, and there is no patching that. Yet these entities are the ones that actually carry out every action and bear every consequence.

If we want to use an analogy to help reach some initial understanding, that is good. But if we want to take the thing we compared to as a model for solving real problems, then besides being inefficient, we may be wrong by a mile without even knowing it.

Analogy also brings a fatal problem: it forces us to choose a threshold to separate the "similar" from the "dissimilar". Once this logic is applied to people, concrete people are split into different groups, and the groups automatically repel one another over the "dissimilar" parts, even though they have far more in common (we are all human, at least, right?).

Combined with abstraction, this gets worse still. The group is an abstraction of the individual, leading to overgeneralization and stereotypes, which easily turn difference into opposition and enmity. The abstraction of groups also makes people seem alien and strange. We lose the ability to empathize and no longer try to understand and communicate; we ignore explanations from other angles, choose sides and apply double standards, and the opposition gradually polarizes, with consequences that are hard to calculate (they deserve to be wiped out; how could they possibly be human beings like us, with flesh and blood, with families, with joys and sorrows, with dreams?).

At this point this essay seems to have reached a conclusion. Abstraction and analogy both have some benefits as we try to understand and solve very complex problems such as epidemics and wars, but if we rely on them too much, we can go badly wrong. Some complexity cannot be simplified; we have to concentrate and chew through it. It is the concrete events, the concrete people, the concrete difficulties and suffering; they come first. If we cannot pay attention to the concrete, check it and analyse it, we will be blinded by abstraction and misled by analogy, and what we end up with is a noisy world where everyone is expressing themselves, siding with their own and attacking the rest, sacrificing the concrete for the abstract. Beneath the fine words, people are still bleeding.

Remember that on that building we all know, the words "the great unity of the peoples of the world" are written. What a beautiful vision. I believe no one truly opposes it, but because of differences in subjective factors (culture, values) and objective ones (interests, old scores from history), it is extremely hard to achieve. And behind the abstraction "the peoples of the world", are there not concrete people like you and me?

If we, as concrete people, all blindly seek simplification, if in thinking about problems and expressing opinions we cannot come down to concrete people and events, cannot hold to one standard as we try to understand and communicate, to seek common ground while setting differences aside, to make this abstract vision concrete, then we can expect even less that the world will move in a good direction. We may even see these pointless expressions bring greater division and conflict instead. If that is so, what is all our expression, which fills this whole age, for?

If we have no hope for the world's progress, then expression is a waste, and not in keeping with the essence of "laziness". If it is only to grab a sense of belonging and respect in social life, could we find some more harmless way? If we really do hope for something, then we cannot be lazy: we should do things that actually matter, and if expression is necessary, do our best to make it beneficial and harmless. Whether it is taking sides, promoting, explaining or joking, if we know full well the harm our expression may cause and still insist on squandering the right of free expression, or deliberately push the other way, then we need only remember that things happening can also be put down to human stupidity, or malice, and in this world where everything bears on everything else, you and I cannot always stay out of it.

So many threads, and what made it onto the page is only half-formed. Forgive me.

item.title: My 2021 in Pictures
item.description:
My 2021 in Pictures

Ordinary Days

The last notes of winter had not yet faded, and the spring sunshine was already showing through. The pandemic changed the course of our lives, but not all of it for the worse. The pandemic, together with a few other coincidences, ended up letting me work remotely from my hometown for a full year and a half. Every day and every hour of it was so ordinary, and yet so worth cherishing. Without the pandemic, these ordinary days, and many of the moments I mention below, might never have happened at all.

At the Ceremony

In an age when we are so far apart and yet so close, how many good friends' weddings can one person make it to? I was very happy to take part in, and witness, this one-of-a-kind moment. What remains: glints of light, glimpses in flight.

The Snow Mountain Trip

Right after that came my first-ever trip to a snow mountain. The journey to the summit was like a life in miniature, with every flavour in it. If you are not sure how to approach life, perhaps give it a try. For me, the deepest lesson was that the boundless view at the top would be pale and feeble indeed without every second along the way to hold it up.

With Fluffball

In 2020, I met a little bulbul in early summer and parted from it in autumn. What I didn't expect was that in the early summer of 2021, as if the world had arranged it on purpose, I would meet one of its close relatives, but this time the parting came sooner and hurt more. Meeting is happiness and parting is pain; there is a time for meeting and a time for parting, and probably everything in the world has these two sides. I know that, materially speaking, these feelings are only biochemical reactions: oxytocin, dopamine, and the storms of electrical signals they set off in the brain, complex but not mysterious. But it is precisely because of these feelings that we can be said to be vividly alive. I think I will always miss these lovely lives I have met and parted from.

The Way Back

After that parting came another parting, but it was also a return. "Return" is an interesting word: what kind of destination do you have to reach before it counts as a return? I think it depends on whether the destination holds a life you know, one that goes on day after day, plain and ordinary and reassuring. And something like the pandemic overturned the ordinary. It turned many things we took for granted, things we could do with a lift of the hand, into brand-new challenges, and made the familiar strange, turning a spacious airport, for instance, into a maze of checkpoint after checkpoint. As it did fourteen years ago, this reminded me once again that the ordinary is the least ordinary thing of all.

Clouds, Sea and Sunset

Even scenery like clouds, the sea and sunsets is the same: they don't seem like things that change easily, yet what you see is never the same twice. On the scale of the whole universe, even the sun is like a flower that blooms for a single night, or as tiny and brief as a bacterium on that flower. Everything is spray thrown up from a sea of chaos, there for an instant and never to be repeated.

The Exhibition Serendipity in the Street

Some of that spray we are lucky enough to record, so that it can be retold, and then it becomes a story. Like what this exhibition (which I came across by chance) recorded: during the pandemic, people of all sorts of backgrounds, brought together by chance, travelling from different corners of Hong Kong by different means of transport to the same street corner to kick a shuttlecock. Baffling, but utterly romantic.

My First Camping Trip in Hong Kong

Like the memories before it, this camping trip was a wonderful experience of the same kind. However much we prepare in advance, we can only roughly steer what comes after. Looking back, nearly everything was improvised on the spot, and yet it all came so naturally, like this campfire. Who would have thought that on a lonely island there would be so much firewood, washed up from who knows where and dried out who knows when, waiting for us to pick it up and use it?

Thirty

It was by the light of that night's campfire, too, that I greeted my thirtieth birthday. Just three days before, because of a chance need at work, I had also got a photo to keep as a memento. The ancients said that at thirty one takes one's stand. But what is it that one stands on? I think the most important thing is to set one's heart firm.

The Last Hike of 2021

In the four months and more since I came back to Hong Kong, I have walked many different hills with many different people. The last hike of 2021 was Ma On Shan, wrapped in cloud and mist. I lugged a drone all the way up, huffing and puffing, but couldn't get a single shot of blue sky and white clouds. Recently I came across the name of a radio programme, On a Clear Day (在晴朗的一天出发, literally "Setting Out on a Clear Day"). But setting out on a day that isn't clear (in the figurative sense) is really nothing to worry about, because however thick the clouds, beyond them is still the boundless universe. Everything has its own flow, accidental and yet natural. For those of us in the midst of it, besides good health and being able to eat and sleep well, the most important and hardest thing to come by is probably a calm, clear state of mind, the spirit of ichigo ichie: this one time, this one meeting.

item.title: On the Value of War
item.description:
On the Value of War

I finished All Quiet on the Western Front today. War stories always stay with me. On the battlefield and off it, the most beautiful things and the ugliest things always bloom at the same time, but in the end all of it passes.

The history of war may be longer than the history of humanity. Look at the ancient apes in 2001: A Space Odyssey: no sooner had they learned to use a bone as a tool than they started killing each other with it. A tool, after all, if it is not used to create something, will surely be used to destroy. The "high-EQ" answer is that destruction is a means and creation is still the end, and that is one hundred percent correct. Things are not created out of nothing; matter and energy are conserved, and to build something you have to break something. The two are simply two sides of one coin, things passing from one pattern to another, the ordinary flow of all things, nothing to marvel at.

But this is plainly the view of a detached onlooker, one that doesn't put people first and has no feeling in it. Once anything enters a human heart, nothing escapes a value judgment. Take the "three views" people in China often talk about: a view of the universe, a view of life and a view of values. The first is how we understand the world and the second how we understand ourselves; both seem to step back and look at things in themselves. Only the third brings in human nature and motive. What is good and what is bad: in a given situation (the universe), how do I, as myself (life), choose (values)?

People make choices all the time: what to have for lunch today, whether this plan is better or that one, where to travel once the pandemic is over, whom to have kids with. Choosing is judging value. Value is an abstraction people arrive at by weighing things; without a human point of view it doesn't really exist, and the world would not end because of that (a worldview might). The question is: if value doesn't have to exist in nature, why did we evolve to think about it every day? Anyone who took high school biology will find this a silly question. Natural selection: life puts the continuation of the species first, and the pressure of the environment pushes living things to seek benefit and avoid harm, to get the best chance of carrying on. So the reason is biological. Humans have it, animals have it, even covid-19 has it. Humans really aren't that special; we are no different from a salted fish, just surviving (just putting food on the table).

At this point someone may jump out and say: you traitor to humankind, talking nonsense with your eyes wide open, have you forgotten Maslow's hierarchy of needs? Eating and surviving are only the most basic physiological and safety needs. We also have belonging, esteem and self-actualization, and that is human nature rising above biology.

Yes. Not wanting to be a traitor to humankind just yet, I too hope that some higher values shine within human nature, the ones that get humans classed as higher animals. Then here is the problem. In a world where all beings are equal and only survival counts, we can put everything we do down to our need to survive. To survive, people can pick up a bowl and eat, or throw the bowl at someone; to survive, people can build spaceships, or clubs; to survive, people can farm and herd, and can also kill any plant, animal or non-living thing they want to kill, including people, of course. If there is anything we haven't killed, it can only be because we can't kill it yet, or because it has nothing to do with survival. If survival is the only value, then taking someone else's survival for your own survival makes a world that is cruel yet fair, and surviving in it is justice.

Now say we do have values beyond survival: the ground under that justice starts to shake. Because now there is another possibility: taking someone else's survival for a value other than your own survival. Remember that the levels of Maslow's pyramid mean something. The lower the level, the more basic the need and the more it must be met first; the need to survive, for example, ranks above self-actualization. If a person A takes B's survival for A's own self-actualization, do you think B would find that fair? Many religions draw a sharp line between killing to survive and killing for pleasure (These violent delights have violent ends), perhaps also to keep a fairness that treats people, and other living things, alike.

Fairness comes from a single standard. For A, unless A rearranges the pyramid and puts some other need above survival, that is, unless A is ready to give up life for righteousness, A cannot justify putting A's other needs above someone else's need to survive, because that would be a double standard.

Giving up life for righteousness (舍生取义, an idiom from Mencius) is, in the low-EQ version, suicidal behavior (which suddenly reminds me that many religions also forbid suicide). The "righteousness" (义) here usually stands for needs that answer to values beyond the individual: the values of a group, of a society.

The word "righteousness" in the idiom already shows that people see this behavior in a positive light, for these reasons:

  1. These "people" belong to the group and benefit, directly or indirectly, from the act, so they feel its value most. It should also be easy to find a measure showing that it pays: for example, sacrificing one person costs 5 points and saving a thousand people earns 1,000.
  2. Breaking the natural priority of the hierarchy of needs is itself extremely hard. Acts like this mark the edges of human nature and have aesthetic value, and that value holds both inside and outside the group: two armies at war whose heroes admire each other is no rare story.

Ah, I'm tired of writing, so I'll stop here for now. A few things I think are worth thinking about further:

  1. Going from the individual to the group, this is reasonable within one group, but across several groups the argument is back where it started. And because groups are involved, hatred forms chains, so war becomes something that never ends
  2. Whether my own standard (my priority of needs) can be imposed on others. This probably touches on the definition of freedom
  3. Where does the value of war really lie?
  4. How are the justice and injustice of a war actually measured?
  5. People in war: smallness, alienation and not being understood, and the good parts such as comradeship --> in fact this part, along with my discontent with this imperfect world, is what I most wanted to get off my chest when I had just finished the book
  6. How can war be avoided?

P.S. Starting from the gloom I felt after finishing one book, I have really dug myself a huge hole. As a science person, I feel rather unschooled in all this.

Douban: All Quiet on the Western Front

item.title: On Expression
item.description:
On Expression

I think people lose the urge to express themselves very easily. You can list any number of reasons, but in the end they all come down to economics: the return on investment is too low => more trouble than it's worth.

  • Investment: expressing yourself means putting in time and energy, organising a little order out of chaos, while not expressing yourself is plainly the direction of least resistance, the natural one, the one in which entropy increases;

  • Return: ask yourself honestly, can you express anything of value? The world is noisy enough already. There is no shortage of voices wiser than yours, clearer than yours, more extreme than yours, or simply louder than yours.

So why not spend a wage slave's scant remaining free time and scant remaining energy lying flat in comfort? And so most people always choose silence.

In fact nobody is truly silent. It's just that most of what we say exists only in the office, at the dinner table and in bed, and these are all private channels. Private means safe, and closeness breeds likeness. People in a private channel always find it easier to talk to each other, because you have so much in common that you needn't lay out at length a concept that is even slightly abstract; a knowing look will do. Even when you run into something you can barely put into words yourself, you only need to add "you know" to get past it, easy and stress-free. Nor do you need to worry much about saying something stupid, something shocking, or a thought that isn't really a thought at all. As long as no tangle of interests is involved that could mean what you say "may be recorded" or "used as evidence in court", it's just casual talk. Words once spoken are like that other thing one lets out: they pass, and that's that (case closed).

And the public channel, as distinct from the private ones? Even if what you face is a sheet of paper (most likely an electronic one) and not a crowd holding rotten eggs or flowers or both, you feel a kind of pressure at every moment. How will your readers, listeners and viewers understand, regard and judge (see the questions people keep asking on Zhihu) everything you express? And the internet has given everyone the power to give feedback instantly. So you feel you may have a duty to express every bit of your thinking and every trace of your feeling more clearly, trying as far as you can to sync and resonate with the strangers in your head. Unfortunately our ability to communicate is still far from having evolved anywhere near perfection, which is why a thousand people have a thousand Hamlets.
