So, alone, I let myself go completely, singing and walking and swaying, lost in it. The roads with no cars and no people seemed especially wide with just me on them; now and then I even walked down the middle of the road, minding no one.

I let the shadows of trees and the sunlight flicker across my eyelids, let the cool wind tousle my hair and blow my coat open, let the music play on shuffle while I sang and danced along. Monotonous? Not at all. I walked in circles on the dry grass at the roadside like a drunk to scrape off the mud stuck to my shoes; wherever I saw a fork I picked the one I liked, walked till there was no road left, turned back and tried again; I even smiled at myself in understanding. So I still have me, this soul that still holds a certain innocence and curiosity towards the world and towards life. The road was like a blank videotape, and I spent three hours recording on it a stretch of time free of all agitation and constraint.

When the mind is let go, when the body is let go, when the soul is let go, the scenery along the way becomes marks in memory that can't be erased. As I walked, I gradually felt that this place was no longer as strange as before. It isn't an inn; it belongs to me too, it's also a home of mine. This time I wasn't a lonely onlooker; I blended quietly into this world, listening to her birdsong, listening to her heartbeat. I also gradually felt that if I don't take that step forward myself, I'll never know what lies ahead on the road. The world is so big, and where you haven't walked, it's a wasteland. But while you walk the road, you can try to believe there will keep being surprises waiting ahead for you. Embrace the world, and only then will the world embrace you.

2012.02

item.title: Numbers
item.description:
Numbers

Walking towards the sea.

2017.06

The Chinese opens with a line from Bibi Zhou's song "Numbers" (号码), about looking for one person in a crowd. It is on the Chinese version of this page and is not translated here.

December, and nearly its last week. Eating, revising, staying up all night on a competition, watching all sorts of films. But my feelings have no way out.

In fact, reading other people's writing and watching other people's stories doesn't release what's knotted up inside me; it only piles more tangled feelings on top.

The street lamps don't seem to be on much. The night is a bit dark, the wind a bit strong; whatever skin is exposed stings a little with cold. I walk on alone, in silence.

My inner feelings plainly have no way to be expressed, yet people say: look at you, making waves online every day, clearly doing very well, very happy; the odd troubled sentence that shows up is replaced a few minutes later by the next lively thought.

In all kinds of books and films, when someone suddenly finds themselves standing in an empty, silent house, they always open their mouth and call out, "Is anyone there?" But if someone lives alone in it for a long time, the strangeness wears off, and they start talking to themselves, or chattering away to lifeless objects. The smallest new thing becomes the best topic of conversation, only the person they are talking to is themselves. Even if other people are not far away, for this person they might as well not exist.

On the way, my MP3 player shuffled to "Numbers". A song that once felt new has turned out to be so old.

Numbers probably have something to do with loneliness. To the left and to the right there are countless numbers, very much alike. But a number is a string of digits, absolutely different from every other. Even if it is related to other numbers, the relation is strictly logical or physical, with nothing else mixed in, because a thin little number cannot carry anything else. That's why characters in stories who have only a code name are often so lonely: such a person can be written down with a scrap of paper and a pen, and to erase them, to wipe them out, so that from then on it is as if they never existed, is as easy as turning your hand.

So many people in the world, adding up to a number so large you might not count to it in a lifetime, and each person is just one tiny point in it. To prove who you are, all it takes is an ID card number; to be enrolled at school, a student number; online, a user ID. In how many people's minds am I only a serial number, passer-by A, B, C, ABC123?

There's a line in Kara no Kyoukai (The Garden of Sinners):

We live in a world so vast and so rich, yet have no real sense of being in it.

Standing on a rooftop looking down on the bustle of the whole world, I am plainly standing right here, and yet it's as if I'm floating in the air. Between the all and the one, between the world and myself, what is it that separates us, transparent and yet unbreakable?

Having tasted the loneliness inside all this noise, I understand even better how hard it is to find someone. In Turn Left, Turn Right, a single sudden shower almost blurs a happy future, and one small habit almost keeps two people living on either side of one wall from ever meeting. The song's refrain makes everyone a number, brushed past and forgotten. Yet in the roar of this great torrent, I could feel the breathing of two or three people, and sense each other's heartbeats. So whether or not we are now at opposite ends of the earth, whether these relationships go sour or grow into something higher over the long time to come, I already have nothing to regret.

The world uses the cruellest methods to put me to the test and teach me to cherish.

Leaving behind all of time's tricks and slanders, I believe that if I keep walking forward, what I leave at the end will be more than a number.

2011.12

item.title: Nightscape
item.description:
Nightscape

On the big school bus back to the Jiangning campus, I was lucky: I got the single seat beside the driver, with a huge glass windscreen in front of me, practically a panorama.

There were specks of grime on the glass, but it was clear enough for the driver to drive steadily, and clear enough for me to peer out at Nanjing in the early-winter night.

If not for this chance, I don't know when I would ever have spent several dozen minutes on something so meaningless. Speaking of meaning, what is "meaning", anyway? If I hadn't caught the last seat on this bus, if night hadn't fallen, I don't know when I would have spent several dozen minutes watching streams of neon fade along the way, with the silhouettes of crowds moving through them; watching countless orange halos of street lamps flicker on and off, half hidden by overpasses and road signs; watching two rows of street lamps wind away along the road. Nor do I know when I would have come to feel this: however solid a thing is, you can always find somewhere in it an abstract beauty; however fixed and unchanging a thing is, you can always find an angle from which it has a flowing beauty.

Lately I've been playing an indie game called Eufloria (its Chinese name means "Fungus World"). It is like an abstraction of reality: it pulls out the basic elements of how life arises, develops and struggles, and rebuilds them simply. Simple, but never dull. Good roots and a good trunk give a tree the nourishment it needs, and it will always grow the most magnificent branches and leaves, then flower and bear fruit. Mathematical modelling, sand-table simulations, building systems of knowledge: the principle is much the same. From one to the ten thousand things, from the infinitely small to the infinitely vast.

And the relation between the fixed and the flowing is one of the most basic questions in philosophy; no need to say more.

Back to where we were: what, after all, is meaning? The question seems too hard to answer, or perhaps you can first add some qualifiers to narrow the discussion, such as the meaning of life (life in the general sense, as distinct from a human life), or the meaning of a human life? That qualifier still seems too broad, so if we add "journey", does that sound more practical? Still too broad; then let's make it the meaning of the journey "on the big Jiangning-campus school bus, I was lucky: I got the single seat beside the driver, with a huge glass windscreen in front of me, practically a panorama". How about that?

Hang on, didn't I say earlier that this was a meaningless thing to do? But if we can't even work out what "meaning" itself is, how can we use it to describe a property of anything else? All right then, tell me: what is "meaning"? It seems we overlooked something. If you don't know the most general sense of a word, then however you restrict it you still can't know it, because the word is the only thing at the centre of your attention; narrowing the range only snips off part of that centre. Tell me: if the whole leopard isn't in front of you, how can you glimpse one of its spots through a tube?

So approaching the question head-on seems hopeless. Why not come at it from the other side? If we can rule out as many wrong answers as possible, we can at least get a little closer to the truth. So what is not meaning? Though you and I are always going on about things being "meaningless", meaningless and not-meaning seem to be two different things; we can't use meaningless things to stand for "not meaning". More discouraging still, at root we can't say anything has no meaning at all, because whatever exists is reasonable, so it always has some meaning. And what is not meaning? You'll find, oh no, that from the other side things are even worse. If you want to prove that a thing is that thing, how can you list, one by one, everything that isn't it? Even if you can name some, you can't carry this approximation through, because the things that are "not it" are infinite in number, and cannot be enumerated.

Well, if you haven't given up reading by now, it seems it's time our questioning gave up. We've thought a great muddle of things and seem to have got not a single (what?) thing out of it, but here at least we haven't copied our maths teachers, who would stare at the word "meaning" for a few seconds and then say, "A definition is a definition, there's no reasoning to it, so don't split hairs." Doesn't doing things differently like this make a new kind of "meaning"?

After going round in so many circles, we find that although we can't really grasp it in our hands, all through the process we could in fact dimly sense what "meaning" means. This really is a marvellous thing. Could this be what is called ideology, a form of consciousness that is the plainest kind of knowing and understanding of everything in the world?

Perhaps this is the chaotic nature of the "real". In physics we keep raising the precision of measurement through methods, instruments and even theory; in daily life we use cameras with ever more pixels to take pictures ever closer to reality; probability theory tells us that repeating something under the same conditions brings us closer to some true value... We are always searching for the real, closing in on it, yet in fact, after hundreds and thousands of years of science, we still can't do this seemingly simple thing, and instead sigh more and more over how elusive the real is. The "real" seems to lie on an asymptote of our journey: we can get closer and closer, a tiny bit at a time, but never arrive. Einstein once said something to the effect that any single leaf drifting down outside the window is enough to make humanity sigh at how powerless science is. So at last we understand why, in a classic science-fiction story, humans fear and revere a stone slab that, however far human technology advances, always measures exactly the same length (the only difference being an ever longer string of "0"s at the end of the number). It gives them the illusion that the civilization that vanished long ago is itself "the real"; this fear comes not from an accumulation of quantity but from an ultimate gap in quality. Fortunately, if quantum theory, which already exists in reality and is still developing, is really correct, we can say with confidence that if the humans in the story could keep their science developing without end, then one day that string of zeros would be ended by some digit from 1 to 9, because the "real" does not in fact exist.

Actually I'm more inclined to say that the real exists only within chaos; what keeps us from touching it is only the nature of chaos, and we can't say it doesn't exist just because we can't see it or grasp it. By now I've more or less explained "chaos" as I understand it. And why talk about "chaos" at all? What is it meant to explain?

The most incredible thing within chaos: "order".

It is chaos's natural enemy, and yet it exists within chaos: a flower that should never have been able to exist in the black turbulence. But it does exist, and that's why I call it a flower, because it is too beautiful a miracle, blooming in this uncertain world.

So let's go back to the last sentence of the third paragraph: "...From one to the ten thousand things, from the infinitely small to the infinitely vast." If the universe is chaotic, its total entropy can only rise, and space-time always tends towards disorder, then doesn't local negative entropy appear for no reason at all? Perhaps you can still explain it with "chaos": since it is chaos, even "chaos" itself is disordered, and anything can happen.

We keep talking about "self-organization": self-organization in physics, self-organization in chemistry... In the end we find that life is the most marvellous self-organization of all, because it is not only material. From the chaotic real arise finite steady states; then these finite steady-state bodies turn out, in the end, to be able to perceive themselves, to perceive an existence of infinite depth, and to build bridges, create radiance, step by step approaching the limit in the dark of chaos, even trying to rebuild nature's fractals out of finite constructions. From doing it without knowing it can't be done, to doing it knowing full well it can't be done. Is this the most ultimate explanation of "meaning"?

What shouldn't happen, happens: we call it a "miracle".

The orange street lamps along the way flowed and changed endlessly through the dark of space and time, as if finite things were turning into the infinite "real". Reality glinted in the crack between stability and turmoil, and the night was so beautiful that humble little I could not breathe.

2011.11

item.title: Serenity
item.description:
Serenity

At ease in motion and in stillness; balance is what matters most.

2017.06

For a year now, whether busy or idle, I have always felt that what I lack most is serenity. What is serenity? Different people define it differently. So what colour, what smell, what shape is serenity to me?

I ask myself: does serenity just mean quiet, leisurely time? No. As I said, even when I have nothing to do, I still lack serenity. When I'm alone and everything around is quiet and silent, often there's still no serenity. Reading a book I like on my own, sitting with four senses shut and my hearing handed over to music, a few people walking along empty streets at night, laughing now and then, or sitting across from each other in a café in silence: they bring the same degree of serenity.

Quiet and serenity are like loudness and frequency in acoustics: one decides quantity, the other quality. It's like a stick of incense burning quietly, without a sound, but burning all the same, so we can't tell from the incense itself whether there is serenity or not. The measure of serenity is more like the wisp of smoke curling up from it, or rather the scent in the smoke: formless, but really there.

Disturbed; yes, disturbed. When a wind blows, the smoke's shape and colour are thrown into disarray, and the scent is torn to pieces. The wind is formless too. You can't find its cause: where it formed, what path it blew along, who knows. All you know is that there is wind, and it has unsettled the heart.

That's right: something this insubstantial, and yet it keeps affecting our state of mind, really and truly.

Perhaps quiet is not even a necessary condition for serenity. Often, when things are lively, even noisy, I still feel serene. Sometimes I'm plainly in the middle of the world's sounds and colours, yet I feel I'm outside it, calmly watching all the comings and goings, all the trajectories, including my own among them. I used to think this feeling would split me in two; now I feel it is just how things should be, and there should be no pain in it. The dreams my outer self can't reach, the stories it can't tell, can all be realized by my inner self, because the inner self is a whole world belonging to one person. Being alone doesn't mean being lonely, because I clearly feel that a large part of this world consists of things the outer self has brought in, filtered: clean, and utterly serene.

Perhaps you could say that the lack of serenity comes from the outer me taking up too much of my time and leaving the inner me restless. It shows in losing any sure feeling for whatever I do, being unable to tell right from wrong, losing my own values and beliefs, unconsciously following the majority to reduce friction with the outer world, feeling lonely, feeling I'm no longer myself. That is what the Eagles sing about in "Desperado": a life gone flat, without its peaks and valleys. The inner self is so sensitive, allowing no one to peek in, and yet longing so much for common ground and understanding.

And so I feel I can never reach serenity, because the inner self can never beat the outer self, just as spiritual pursuits can never beat material desires, just as smoke and scent, once they rise, are at once thinned out by the time and space around them; this is decided by the basic material makeup of being human. But the inner self is something that never admits defeat, stubborn and unreasonable, so that now and then it makes an unusual decision about something and gives the people around me a real fright. The "usual" it goes against is in fact the outer world, a world made of material foundations and everyone's outer selves. That is probably also why many schools of thought agree that people are solitary by nature: the inner self is such a tsundere thing. It spins its own cocoon and binds itself in it, and knows no peace. It plainly longs for something, yet is afraid of being hurt.

And all we can do is leave ourselves some room as far as we can: to read a book we like on our own, to sit with four senses shut and our hearing handed over to music, or to walk with a few others along empty streets at night, laughing now and then, or to sit across from each other in a café in silence, hoping to come just a little closer to serenity.

I don't really know what I'm writing, or why. Call it a daydream to fight the life I'm living now.

2011.09

item.title: Love and Letting Go
item.description:
Love and Letting Go

Things have their weight.

2017.06

Nanjing's wind has started running wild again.

The magnolias have barely opened and already the ground is covered in white sails, yet look up and they're still in full bloom. It's as if the flowers bloomed too lavishly, too saturated, and couldn't hold on, and so dropped from the branches. The sun is brilliant, and the gap between day and night temperatures has grown, but it all stays within a comfortable range, slightly on the cool side. This is probably what counts as spring in Nanjing. I ought to treasure it.

My mood has had few ups and downs lately; compared with last year I'm much calmer, with more certainty and composure, it seems. Every day goes by step by step; even though there are still plenty of annoying things, on the whole I'm warm and at ease. Thinking of past twists and turns, and of the disaster happening not far away, I should be glad to have such plain, quiet days.

Today before my C programming class I found I'd used up my notebook, and pulled out the last notebook I'd bought in my final year of high school, one I really like. It was empty, not a word in it, because I couldn't bear to use it, because it was a keepsake of that time and of those three people. When class started I sat holding it, lost in thought for a long while, telling myself over and over that old things can carry new things, and that would make it fuller, more worth treasuring. I even considered what name to give it, and what words of remembrance to write on the first page. But in the end I still couldn't bring myself to write in it, because I wanted it to stay pure and unchanged; fuller would be good, of course, but in the end it would also become a jumble. So I took out my old notebook and made do with taking notes on its cover.

But the world is always strange: C, again, was what almost cost me that notebook entirely. After this afternoon's C class came the lab session straight after, from four to eight. So as usual I'd packed some food in my bag to get me through dinner, including the cup of yellow-peach yogurt I order for every day. Programming is brain work, but sometimes it feels just like a detective game, and as you go you get absorbed. So in the breaks I ate only a packet of biscuits and a few pieces of white honey cake, and forgot about the yogurt.

Leaving the computer lab, I went to a get-together of the team we'd recently formed, and we talked about plans for later; the few of us really got going. In high spirits and fully absorbed, I naturally had no idea tragedy had already struck. When we finished and I got up, I found the yogurt in my bag had been squashed out, and naturally nothing inside escaped. I'd always thought this yogurt was so thick it was practically a paste, of excellent quality; you could really use it as a face mask. I never imagined its first trial would be on my advanced maths and information management textbooks, a book of English poetry borrowed from the library and the rest, and of course two notebooks, one new, one old.

On the way back to the dorm, I did some "emergency treatment" with the little tissue I had on me. Things weren't too bad; the new notebook got off fairly lightly as "disaster areas" go. I couldn't help feeling a bit glum, but a moment later my thoughts turned another way, and it struck me as ironic that something I treasured so much had nearly been ruined by my own carelessness, just like that. Cause and effect go round and round, always leaving you moved and helpless. Then I suddenly remembered a passage I'd read not long before. The gist was: you keep many treasured things at home and can't bear to part with them, and over the years they pile up; then one day a fire burns them all to nothing, and after a brief sadness you find that no longer having them makes you feel lighter and freer than having them did.

Just as when I took the books out of my bag, braced for the worst, I found it wasn't nearly as agonizing and torn as I'd been that afternoon. Isn't it often the case that letting go is the more perfect ending?

So I wanted to write this down, as a small insight in life. Perhaps because of the recent magnitude 9.0 earthquake (a disaster is humanity's disaster, not any one country's), when thinking of a title I remembered that I had once meant to write something about '08 (the title I'd settled on then was "Love and Letting Go") but in the end never put it on paper. It came to mind by coincidence, and on reflection it fits what I feel today rather well, so I've simply taken it, which I suppose finally fulfils the idea of putting old things to new use. As for why I chose that title in the first place, time has passed and things have changed, and I've forgotten it entirely. If I remember one day, I can always add a line.

That night,
first drafted to the melody of KOKIA's "Hoshikuzu no Vocalise" (Stardust Vocalise)

2011.03

item.title: Paper and Pen
item.description:
Paper and Pen

When did I stop relying on paper and pen? There's no need to dig deep into that; the answer comes at once. The written word: I've loved it for eight years, at one point so much that I had to carry a little notebook and a pen with me everywhere. When I first fell in love with the written word, Guo Jingming was still a sentimental big boy, and in most people's eyes Han Han was still mostly a rebellious brat. Guo Jingming wrote back then that he liked holding a pen and writing on sheet after sheet of smooth, clean white paper.

I love that feeling too. White paper is spotless; writing on it is like looking in a mirror. Anything affected or untrue, once written down, gives you a strong urge to cross it out. And white paper stands for infinite possibility, as if it could stretch on forever: however far your thoughts can go, the pen can go. Paper is thin, but good paper always has a particular texture to the touch, and what that feeling tells you is not that it has no depth, but that its depth is hard to measure. Close your eyes and imagine the tree this sheet came from, from bud to towering height, through how much wind and rain, cloud and sun; imagine which light breath of air those fibres first came from, how they grew bit by bit, silently, longer and longer, longer and longer, knitting into nets that are natural and random yet hold hidden rules..... And you can trace it further back, to before this tree, to the infinitely distant past. What grandeur is this, what beauty that exhausts the imagination?

When I write for my own amusement, I usually take out a sheet or two first, not necessarily pure white or of any great quality, but it has to be flat. My first drafts are so scrawled that basically only I can read them. When I finish, I usually put them down wherever, and when I take them out again a while later they're often crumpled; only the occasional one I value especially gets properly put away. Crumpled is all right, but the bottom line is that nothing can be missing, because the next step is to copy the text out carefully onto fresh white paper, revising as I copy. Once revised, it gets put away again, and some time later, if the mood takes me, I may take it out and revise it again. So after all these years, untidy as I am, a drawer of my desk set aside for the purpose is stuffed with all sorts of drafts in a complete jumble.

I used to be a little in love with my own handwriting, though historically it has indeed not received much praise. In fact, whatever the handwriting is like, when characters that belong to you, that stand for your own thoughts and feelings, take shape and line up under your pen on the paper, the satisfaction (or call it achievement) is irreplaceable. And it is precisely because this is unique that it makes you treat every character and every word you're about to write with care, and in the light of this attitude, wrong characters, errors and poor rhetoric naturally dwindle to a minimum. And each sheet of white paper is given a whole new meaning by you, newer than the paper itself, but with a source perhaps even more ancient than the paper's (I have always believed that all things have some transcendent connection, even across the bounds of time and space, so even a new spark may come from the sediment of long ages).

People who write a lot will always have marks built up over the years on their fingers. On my right middle finger, for instance, at the base of the nail on the side where the pen rests, there's a layer of something like a callus but not quite, faintly bluish, and the whole joint bulges a little compared with my left hand. Since everyone holds a pen a bit differently, the hands of those who love to write (好书, with 好 read in the fourth tone, hào, "to love", please note) won't all be like mine, but they're sure to show similar signs. Legend has it that when Lu Yu, the Sage of Tea, dipped his finger in water, the colour of tea would spread from it; so for the ancients who were masters of paper, ink, brush and inkstone, perhaps their calluses bore the colours of gold ink and painting. I described it earlier as something built up over the years; really it's also the sediment of time, and more than that, the growth rings of feeling.

When the ancients wrote, they surely had a whole set of customs. Even in his humble room, Liu Yuxi still had to "tune the plain zither and read the golden sutras" (from his "Inscription for a Humble Room", translated for this page; let's take the two as conditions for each other), not to mention grinding ink, and perhaps also sitting still in meditation, burning incense, bathing and so on. In today's fast-paced life, all this could easily be mocked as fussy formalities, with a whiff of pedantry. But on second thought, rules that fit their time and world are part of culture. People can't break free of rules, just as people can't refuse culture. Of course, "culture" here isn't the "culture" we mean when we sneer at someone for "having no culture"; it is a mode or system of thinking, the root ideas and concepts a group needs to come into being.

Paper and pen have flowed in China's blood for a thousand years, carrying the culture of this ancient land down the veins of history for a thousand years. Many customs and rules arrived in a hurry carrying different cultures, and vanished just as fast, or changed beyond recognition through collision and fusion. But paper and pen have come down through the long ages to the present; once the carriers of culture and civilization, they have themselves become a culture, an eternal, beautiful legend.

Yet this legend, it seems, is also walking the road to extinction, going, going further away.

Without my noticing, there's no longer a sheet of smooth, handsome paper around me, or a fine pen that sits well in my hand. My fingers' memory of pen and paper is gradually being taken apart and eaten away by the layout of keys on a keyboard, and all that endlessly rich meaning, that boundlessly alive spirit, has been swapped for the dry descriptions produced by humanity's clumsy programming languages. Perhaps it's inevitable that paper and pen are replaced, and the new tools do have many advantages, but a beautiful coat can only set off a gorgeous exterior; inside is a huge, worm-eaten hole. People are always like this: for short-term prospects they throw away the treasures of the past, and step by step turn their backs on the spirit that nature spent hundreds of millions of years giving them. Slogans about the future sound very nice, but without a past there's no present, let alone a future.

Watching these words, which have lost their edges like dry grass stripped down to its fibres, go on line after line across the screen, I can't help imagining: if one day paper and pen really do leave people's lives completely, we will surely need some descriptions and records of them to hand down to later generations, and when even these tributes can only be recorded and passed on through arrays of virtual symbols, will there still be a few people who feel even the slightest flutter?

Perhaps the answer is no, because by then paper and pen will have lost even the right to a corner of memory.

That night,

no paper, no pen.

2011.03

item.title: The City I Love
item.description:
The City I Love

One city, one set of memories; one person, one road, city after city: the luck of living in this age.

2017.06

The night rain drips, drips, striking the dark. My hometown, on my last settled night, gives me this great gift. I don't know what I'm feeling right now, nervous or excited; anyway, I've tossed and turned for ages and can't sleep. I always say I adapt well, yet faced with change I can never stay calm; usually I'm tossing and turning days in advance, and when I do sleep it's a pile-up of tangled dreams. My thoughts are always like this, surfacing layer on layer like dreams, never holding together in one line; that's one reason I've been so slow to really try writing fiction.

Mianyang, my hometown. I often feel my origins are tangled and complicated, that I have no real sense of belonging, but really that's just a pose of being different, a conceit. Every time, only when I'm about to leave, like on this last night, or about to come back, do I realize how deeply attached I am to this land. Grown animals are never as easy to tame as young ones. When I was little, some friends left Mianyang for big, glittering, beautiful cities; once gone, after a few trips back and forth, they settled their hearts in their new nests, with new lives and new circles you could look at but never enter. And me? Eighteen years and nine months, every one of them given to this land, and the dreams of my childhood are just like the thousand years of richness and security of the Sichuan Basin.

Perhaps the mother who gives birth to you really does count for less than the mother who raises you (though of course, for most people, they are the same mother), just as there is always a place in the human heart where matter cannot beat spirit. And when we say "blood", how could that mean the genetic chain passed down through the generations? And those so-called views of race: aren't they just feudal belief in another guise?

The sound of the night rain has thinned, but the drops are still falling in my heart. I love Mianyang. Not just like it: liking is only a simple pleasure, but love is immensely heavy, a mix of every flavour. As someone once said: you may not like Nanshan, but you must love Nanshan; you may like America, but you must not love America. I agree deeply with the first half. Nanshan, my high school, stirs all kinds of feelings in me at once. My three years there were one hardship after another, wind and rain without end, nature's revenge and the wickedness of people's hearts, and with them came rapid growth and transformation. Of course, the views I came upon in a hurry after the skies cleared, even with only a very, very short time to take them in, will stay with me for the rest of my life. The me of today has said goodbye to the golden mean I used to put on, faces the world's pain and love openly, and judges people and events fairly. Nanshan gave me three years unlike most people's. I could never say, and couldn't say, whether I liked it or hated it, but now I can say honestly: I love Nanshan.

In the same way, I love Mianyang too. Mianyang has its faults. It isn't deep enough: you can't dig into it the way you read the drifting clouds and smoke of Nanjing's Six Dynasties. Nor is it shallow enough: the traces of farming civilization have faded fast these past years, while industrial civilization hasn't yet reached any height worth noticing. But I love Mianyang. So what if other places are ancient capitals, or at the cutting edge? What's on the page can never match even a single year of vivid memories in the heart. Each place's water and soil raise their own people; some things grow up together with people, and only those who live there know its scenery best. So all comparison becomes nothing but a silly sulk. A nest of gold or silver can't compare with the nest in your own heart; wherever the heart rests is the most beautiful place. That is a fact that can never change.

And yet, however clearly I understand all this, I am still only a child, and going far from the hometown I love always leaves me sighing. Autumn came early to my hometown this year. Every year, the day the leaves fall back to their roots is just when people go off to the ends of the earth. Fate plays its tricks; no wonder the ancients hit upon what falling leaves and parting people have in common.

Leaving the city I love. The night is deep, the rain has stopped, and I'm sleepy too. When day has broken and night has fallen again, it will be time to pack my bags and set off.

Nanjing, a strange city, and some strangers, not far off, are waiting for me. I'm leaving. I'm coming.

2010.09

item.title: Stars (Missing the Long Runs of Boarding-School Days, or Something Else)
item.description:
Stars (Missing the Long Runs of Boarding-School Days, or Something Else)

Twenty-five and a half years. Since change is unavoidable, enjoy it, and ride it.

2017.06

When the starry sky over the city slowly dims, where can the dreams of childhood be found?
— Epigraph

Since there are only twenty minutes left, I might as well write a little.

The sky has been fairly clear these last few days. Although the temperature keeps dropping, the padded coat of cloud, like tattered cotton wadding, that stands for winter has broken up again (I'd thought winter was coming early). The hem of this autumn swept past in a flash; the weather really is getting harder and harder to read. But I never expected that I could still see the starry sky I've missed for so long. It's really lovely.

I've been busy lately, as if the east wind had wrung out all the lazy moisture stored in my days, leaving them tight, without a single crack to slip into. At least for now, only the endless "bedtime long run" lets me cast off all my jumbled thoughts, all the tongue-twisting theorems, all the twisting, turning three-dimensional structures of molecules. Just running: whatever the purpose before I start, once I've started, none of the reasons matter any more. Just run, take in oxygen, give off heat, sweat.

Whenever I've run three or four laps and I'm warming up and panting, a strange scene often surfaces in my mind: ATP molecules one after another, in a jumble, jostling and shoving, snapping apart with a "crack-crack-crack", sending energy into my cells, my joints, every muscle that moves, while most of what goes unused is finally lost with the sweat, rising from my pores as white steam. So it seems that even like this, I still can't completely forget the things I'm trying hard to forget.

As I ran, I happened to glance up at the night sky, and something stirred faintly in my heart. Stars, one, two, three, four, stars I hadn't seen for so long, blurry and half-visible in my memory. I wasn't wearing my glasses, but I could make out many of them with my naked eye as it is now. Their rough outlines stirred thread after thread of a familiar, fond feeling. In a daze, I felt I had come to the sports field for these tiny, tiny points of starlight from the start. They aren't bright, but they dot the black curtain of night and bring a gentle, peaceful feeling. As I gazed, the heat all over me seemed to fade little by little, and everything grew still, my body temperature and the usual irritable itch in my heart alike. The rushing about of these few days suddenly felt far away, washed fainter and fainter, like a dream tightly wrapped in exhaustion, whose details, once you wake, have almost all been devoured by the dream-eating baku.

In the haze, what grew clearer was my childhood love for that ocean overhead, my devotion to star after star, my tracing of constellation after constellation. Compared with a person, the stars are almost eternal, and yet just then I suddenly felt that sixteen years was a far greater distance. Because the dream that once shone so brightly has long been buried far too deep by that hurried distance, and has long since lost all its light. I couldn't help feeling a little wistful. A sense of loss, like the starlight overhead right now: faint, but clear and hard to wipe away.

Like someone walking down a mottled road, countless strange and dazzling things flashing past; looking back, they find that the road they came by has long been forgotten, and there's no turning back. And the hourglass of time, in this brief moment of gazing, has quietly let fall one more grain of sand.

2008.10
